# Orientation-separated moment dual and exact axial tails

This note records a corrected sufficient criterion for the ordinary weighted stationary-section problem for homothetic centrally symmetric profiles. It proves the reduction and the finite dual characterization, not the universal scalar inequality. The counterexamples to a single common moment multiplier in `candidate 197c4420ab5b2852` do not refute this corrected criterion.

## 1. Common planar component data

Let d=m+1>=2 and let r be positive and concave on [a,b], a<0<b. On the planar body |x|<=r(z), define the measure with density

    f(x,z)=r(z)^(m-1)/2.

Its mass is V=int_a^b r(z)^m dz. For s>=0 put

    P(s)=int 1_{z+s x>=0} f,
    C(s)=int delta(z+s x) f,
    M(s)=int z delta(z+s x) f.

The coarea convention is integration over the indicated line divided by the raw normal length. Thus C is positive and M is its unnormalized vertical first moment. In particular M(0)=0.

The corrected criterion seeks a single c and SEPARATE real numbers lambda_L,lambda_U such that

    P(s)-c C(s) >= gamma_d V+lambda_L M(s),
    P(s)-c C(s) <= (1-gamma_d)V+lambda_U M(s)       (1)

for all s>=0. There is no requirement that lambda_L=lambda_U.

## 2. Why this criterion is sufficient for the actual common-profile family

Let D be any centered centrally symmetric convex m-body, and let

    K={(X,z):a<=z<=b, X in r(z)D}.

Fix a nonhorizontal cap normal, normalized up to orientation to (v,1). The marginal of uniform D in the direction v is even and unimodal. After normalization to probability, it is a mixture of uniform laws on centered intervals [-R,R]. This layer representation follows directly by integrating the nonnegative Stieltjes measure -2R dphi(R), including a possible jump at the outer endpoint, where phi is the even nonincreasing marginal density.

For a layer of radius R, the substitution x=R X gives exactly the measure f above, and the cap slope becomes s=|v|R. The normalization is common: every layer has mass V. Hence the cap's mass and raw vertical coarea, divided by |D|, are the averages of P(s) and C(s) under the same layer probability law. Its vertical section first moment, divided by |D|, is the average of M(s). An individually centered actual section therefore has average M equal to zero. This uses actual section centering; it does not assert centering of the layers.

Both inequalities (1) consequently pass separately to this actual cap. For the reversed cap, the mass complements and the signed vertical coarea reverses. The same common c therefore supplies its corresponding lower inequality. The two moment multipliers need not agree, since their respective averages vanish separately before different cap orientations are combined.

Now take any actual finite menu with centered sections and response balance sum theta_i S_i u_i=0. Reflection of each cap across X=0 cancels its horizontal gradient component without changing its mass, section area, or vertical gradient. For a unit normal u_i with nonzero vertical component b_i, the raw vertical coarea is |b_i|S_i, and its signed version is b_i S_i. Multiplying the resulting cap inequalities by theta_i and summing cancels the c correction by the vertical component of the given normal balance. Caps with b_i=0 capture exactly half of every centered symmetric fiber and require no correction. Thus (1), if proved for this r and d, implies

    sum_i theta_i |K intersect H_i|/|K| >= gamma_d.

This is an ordinary continuous conditional theorem. No mixed-integer transfer is asserted.

## 3. Exact finite characterization by centered slope pairs

For any finite list of slopes s_i, write (P_i,C_i,M_i) for their data. A zero-moment mixture is a probability vector nu satisfying sum nu_i M_i=0. It yields the closed interval

    I(nu)=[(sum nu_i P_i-(1-gamma_d)V)/(sum nu_i C_i),
           (sum nu_i P_i-gamma_d V)/(sum nu_i C_i)].  (2)

There exist c,lambda_L,lambda_U satisfying (1) on the finite list if and only if all intervals I(nu) have common intersection. Moreover it suffices to check mixtures supported on a zero-M slope or on a pair with strictly opposite M signs.

Proof. Necessity follows by averaging each inequality separately. For sufficiency, choose c in the intersection. The lower inequality asks for

    lambda_L M_i <= P_i-gamma_d V-c C_i.

Positive M_i give upper bounds on lambda_L and negative M_i give lower bounds. The zero-M conditions follow from (2). Every comparison between one lower and one upper bound is exactly the lower inequality averaged with the unique positive weights canceling that pair's M values. These comparisons hold by (2), so lambda_L exists. The upper inequality gives the same argument independently for lambda_U.

Finally, the zero-moment probability vectors form a finite polytope. Its extreme points have support at most two: a support of size at least three admits a nonzero two-sided variation preserving both mass and moment. Two-point extreme supports must have opposite moment signs, unless both moments vanish, in which case one-point mixtures suffice. Each endpoint in (2) is a linear-fractional function with strictly positive denominator. Its value on any convex combination lies between the values on the combined extreme points, with weights proportional to their denominators. Thus it suffices to check the stated supports. QED.

For infinitely many slopes, zero-moment mixture inequalities remain a valid formulation without an unproved assertion that finite moment multipliers attain a limit. The finite dual alone does not justify such attainment near a vanishing moment or at an unbounded slope.

## 4. Exact tail and derivative identities

Use the increasing projective coordinate u=z/r(z), its reciprocal profile R(u)=1/r(z(u)), and

    w(u)=(R(u)-u R'(u)) R(u)^(-d-1).

Extend w by zero outside the actual transformed axial interval. The change-of-variables proof is in `candidate 9cc7f272d6dd1c14`; it gives V=int w. For s>0, direct substitution yields

    C(s)=(1/(2s)) int_[-s,s] w(u)R(u)du,
    M(s)=(1/(2s)) int_[-s,s] u w(u)du,              (3)

    P(s)=int_(u>s) w(u)du
             +(1/2) int_[-s,s] w(u)du+M(s).        (4)

In particular

    P(s)-M(s)
      =(1/2)[V+int_(u>s)w(u)du-int_(u<-s)w(u)du].  (5)

These identities retain both fully captured and fully missed axial tails, including finite endpoint truncations. Formula (5) shows precisely what survives after a same-orientation mixture cancels its section first moment: the mixture still averages an axial tail asymmetry.

Where derivatives exist, differentiating (4), or the equivalent uniform threshold average, gives

    M(s)=-s P'(s).                                  (6)

Absolute continuity on compact slope intervals away from zero suffices for the integrated version. Formula (6) does not imply that a zero-moment mixture is supported on stationary individual slopes.

## 5. Current exact boundary

The affine-frustum counterexample to a common lambda has M(s)<0 for every s>0. Its cancellation occurred between opposite cap orientations, which the present criterion does not allow. It is therefore not an obstruction to (1).

More generally, there is a complete elementary result whenever M(s) has one strict sign for every finite s>0. In that case the layer representation shows that an actual individually centered section cannot have both nonzero horizontal and nonzero vertical normal components: its average M would have the same strict sign. The remaining horizontal cutting planes z=0 have identical coarea in their two orientations, so vertical normal balance assigns equal total response weights to the two complementary caps. Cutting planes with zero vertical normal capture half of every centrally symmetric fiber. Therefore EVERY actual centered-section balanced menu has mean exactly1/2 under this one-sign hypothesis. No existence or finiteness of the multipliers in (1) is needed for this conclusion.

The double-cone waist calculation in Section6 of `candidate 9cc7f272d6dd1c14` is an explicit geometric instance. The remaining nontrivial scalar comparison must retain profiles whose finite-slope M values have both signs, or whose zero set supports additional centered cap components.

The finite criterion and tail identities are proved. No universal intersection theorem for (2), no universal three-parameter inequality (1), and no deduction of OC are claimed here. Discovery scripts testing finite slope lists are only falsification tools and are not dependencies of any assertion in this note.

## 6. A proved projective coarea bound for every centered mixture

Write r0=r(0)>0. Choose any affine support to r at zero,

    ell(z)=r0+alpha z >= r(z),
    b0=alpha/r0.

Such a finite support exists because zero is interior to the interval of the finite concave function r. Since r is positive on the compact interval, 1+b0 z is uniformly positive there. Then EVERY slope s>=0 satisfies

    int (1+b0 z)^(-d) d sigma_s(z) <= r0^m=C(0),       (7)

where sigma_s is the raw section coarea measure projected onto its z coordinate. It follows in particular that

    C(s)-d b0 M(s) <= C(0).                            (8)

Consequently every probability mixture with average M equal to zero has

    average C(s) <= C(0).                              (9)

No component centering or convexity of the mixed section measure is assumed in these assertions.

Proof. At s=0, sigma_0=r0^m delta_0 and (7) is equality. For s>0 the exact section formula is

    d sigma_s(z)=r(z)^(m-1) dz/(2s)

on E_s={z in[a,b]: |z|<=s r(z)}. The set E_s is an interval because r(z)-|z|/s is concave. Use the increasing change of variable

    q=z/[s(1+b0 z)],   dq=dz/[s(1+b0 z)^2].

For z in E_s,

    |q|<=r(z)/(1+b0 z)<=r0.

Also r(z)^(m-1)<=[r0(1+b0 z)]^(m-1). Since d=m+1, these facts give

    int_(E_s) (1+b0 z)^(-d) r(z)^(m-1) dz/(2s)
      <= (r0^(m-1)/2) int_(q(E_s)) dq
      <= r0^m.

This proves (7), including m=1. The convex function (1+b0 z)^(-d) lies above its tangent 1-d b0 z at zero, so integrating proves (8). Averaging (8) directly proves (9).

Alternatively, averaging (7) first gives a single finite positive measure sigma_bar with mass C_bar and first moment zero. Jensen's inequality for sigma_bar/C_bar makes its projective integral at least C_bar, again giving (9). This version emphasizes that the same affine support is used for every slope.

If b0!=0, the convex denominator function is strictly convex. Thus equality in (9) forces the averaged section measure to be supported at z=0. Every finite slope s>0 has positive section measure on a nontrivial interval about zero. Therefore a probability mixture involving such a slope cannot attain equality in (9) when b0!=0. This strictness has no asserted uniform reserve as slopes tend to zero.

The estimate is a genuine constraint on the centered slope pairs in (2). It does not by itself control their cap masses P, whose exact tail term remains present in (5).

## 7. Exact monotonicity of a projective cap-coarea combination

Use the same support ell(z)=r0(1+b0 z) as in Section6. Then

    F(s):=C(s)+d b0[P(s)-V/2]

is nonnegative and nonincreasing on [0,infinity), with

    F(0)=C(0)+d b0[P(0)-V/2],
    lim_(s->infinity) F(s)=0.                        (10)

In particular every slope, and every probability mixture of slopes, satisfies

    0 <= C(s)+d b0[P(s)-V/2] <= F(0).               (11)

This is not a consequence of merely replacing C by C(0); it retains a common tail quantity and an exact nonnegative loss measure.

Proof. Apply the source-preserving projective chart

    z'=z/(1+b0 z),
    rtilde(z')=r(z)/(1+b0 z).

Its compact axial interval [a',b'] contains zero. The transformed profile is concave: it is the perspective of r under the inverse chart. The supporting inequality gives rtilde<=r0 with equality at zero. Consequently rtilde is nonincreasing along either ray from zero. Extend it by zero outside [a',b'] only for defining the densities below; no global concavity of that extension is asserted.

For s>0 define on [-r0,r0]

    e_s(q)=(1/2) rtilde(sq)^(m-1)
               1_{sq in[a',b']} 1_{|q|<=rtilde(sq)}.

At m=1 the factor rtilde^0 is interpreted only inside the actual interval, where rtilde>0; the density is zero outside it. For each fixed q, e_s(q) is nonnegative, bounded, and nonincreasing as a function of s. Put eta_s(dq)=e_s(q)dq. The exact inverse-chart change of variables gives

    C(s)=int (1-b0s q)^(-d) e_s(q)dq,
    M(s)=int s q(1-b0s q)^(-d-1) e_s(q)dq.         (12)

The denominator is uniformly positive on every actual active support: there s q=z' belongs to the compact interval [a',b'], and

    1-b0 z'=1/(1+b0 z)>0.

Here is a bounded-variation justification that retains support deletions. On any compact slope interval [s1,s2] with s1>0, replace t^(-d) below half this positive lower bound by a positive C1 extension. This changes neither (12) nor the derivative of its weight where e_s is nonzero. The product rule for a C1 function times the bounded monotone function e_s(q) gives, after integrating over q,

    dC(s)=d b0 [M(s)/s] ds - dXi(s),                (13)

where Xi is the nonnegative local measure

    dXi(s)=int (1-b0s q)^(-d) [-d_s e_s(q)]dq.

At a deletion point the denominator is still on the same positive compact range. The chosen extension therefore leaves Xi unchanged. The product rule and Fubini are justified by the uniform density bound and the fact that the variation of each e_s(q) is at most its initial value. This also retains any jumps caused by the original finite axial endpoints.

Using dP(s)=-M(s)ds/s from (6) now cancels the absolutely continuous terms:

    d[C(s)+d b0 P(s)]=-dXi(s).                     (14)

Thus F is nonincreasing. As s tends to zero, ordinary section and cap continuity at the interior source give C(s)->r0^m and P(s)->P(0). For all sufficiently large s, |z|<=s r(z) throughout the original compact interval, since r has a positive minimum. The direct section formula then gives C(s)=O(1/s), while the cap fraction converges by bounded convergence to V/2. Hence F tends to zero. Monotonicity proves (10)--(11). QED.

The complete loss identity is Xi((s,t])=F(s)-F(t), with the usual continuous representatives of C and P. In particular Xi((0,infinity))=F(0). The centered-mixture estimate C_bar<=C(0) remains a separate constraint; (11) alone does not impose the correlation between the averaged cap mass and averaged coarea needed to prove the common interval intersection in Section3.
